A1-A2.headline: Mike Rogers Holds Blackstone Data Fund

pages.text: Mike Rogers, the Republican candidate for Michigan's U.S. Senate seat, is facing scrutiny over his financial ties to the data center industry. According to a financial disclosure filed on July 6, 2026, Rogers holds between $100,001 and $250,000 in the Blackstone Real Estate Income Trust (BREIT). This fund has moved heavily into data centers, which now make up about 29 percent of its holdings.
pages.caption: Illustrative image: Lansing, Michigan skyline 2024

pages.text: Blackstone is also a lead investor in a $16 billion Oracle data center project in Saline Township. For most of his campaign, Rogers was a vocal supporter of data centers, endorsing federal plans to speed up their permitting. However, his position shifted in August, just three days after reports of his Blackstone investment surfaced.

Rogers suddenly called for a one-year moratorium on new data centers, citing concerns about water and power usage. Despite this reversal, he has not sold his stake in the fund, and his campaign has declined to say if he plans to divest. The situation is further complicated by campaign contributions from Blackstone’s CEO, Stephen Schwarzman.

Schwarzman provided $4.5 million to a super PAC supporting Rogers in 2024 and gave the maximum $7,000 directly to his campaign. While these contributions and the investment are legal, critics argue that Rogers faces a textbook conflict of interest. If elected, he would be in a position to influence federal regulations for an industry in which he is personally invested and from which he receives significant financial backing.

pages.text: As Michigan voters prepare for the November 3 election, Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers finds himself at the center of a debate regarding potential conflicts of interest. Financial disclosures from July 6, 2026, reveal that Rogers maintains a stake valued between $100,001 and $250,000 in the Blackstone Real Estate Income Trust (BREIT).
pages.caption: Illustrative image: Lansing, Michigan skyline 2024

pages.text: This investment vehicle has significantly increased its exposure to data centers, which currently account for approximately 29 percent of its portfolio. Concurrently, Blackstone is a primary financier for a $16 billion Oracle data center development in Saline Township. Throughout the early stages of his campaign, Rogers championed the expansion of data center infrastructure, advocating for federal policies to expedite permitting processes while dismissing environmental concerns.

This stance underwent a abrupt transition in August, shortly after public reports highlighted his financial interest in Blackstone. Rogers subsequently proposed a one-year moratorium on new data center projects, attributing the change to a need to protect local communities and utility resources. Nevertheless, the candidate has retained his financial position, and his campaign has remained non-committal regarding potential divestment.

The ethical questions are compounded by substantial financial support from Blackstone’s leadership. Stephen Schwarzman, the firm's CEO, contributed $4.5 million to a super PAC dedicated to Rogers's election in 2024, in addition to a $7,000 direct donation to his campaign committee. While these transactions comply with existing legal frameworks, the optics present a classic conflict of interest.

Should Rogers be elected, he would be tasked with shaping federal policy on taxation, energy, and environmental regulation for an industry that serves as both a personal investment and a source of significant campaign funding. Although Rogers’s pivot against his own holding suggests he is not explicitly steering policy to benefit his portfolio, the structural conflict remains, as he would be positioned to regulate an industry to which he is deeply tied.

pages.text: Many people give money to the same Republican candidates in Michigan. Mike Rogers wants to be a senator. John James wants to be governor. Tom Barrett wants to keep his job in the House. Voters will choose them on November 3. The DeVos family is very important.
pages.caption: Illustrative image: Lansing, Michigan skyline 2024

pages.text: They are from west Michigan. They made money with a company called Amway. They gave about $7.3 million to these three campaigns. They give money directly to the candidates. They also give money to groups called super PACs. These groups spend money to help the candidates win.

A man named Tim Dunn is also important. He is from Texas and works in oil. He gave about $10 million to help Mike Rogers. The DeVos family gave $6 million to help John James. They also gave money to help Mike Rogers and Tom Barrett.

The candidates share some of the same people who help them with money. The DeVos family and other rich people give a lot of money to these campaigns. People wonder if the candidates listen to the voters or the people who give them money.

evidence: — Much of the money behind Michigan's three biggest 2026 Republican campaigns comes from the same donors.
Mike Rogers is running for the open U.S. Senate seat, John James for governor, and Tom Barrett to hold the 7th Congressional District, the Lansing-area House seat he already represents.
Voters across Michigan choose among them in the general election on November 3.
A1-A2.headline: Same Donors Fund Michigan Republican Ticket

pages.text: In Michigan, the 2026 Republican ticket relies on a shared network of wealthy donors. Mike Rogers, who is running for the U.S. Senate, John James, the candidate for governor, and Tom Barrett, who represents the 7th Congressional District, all draw from the same financial sources. Voters will head to the polls on November 3 to decide the outcome of these races.
pages.caption: Illustrative image: Lansing, Michigan skyline 2024

pages.text: The DeVos family of west Michigan is the most prominent contributor. Having built their fortune through Amway, the family has spent decades supporting Republican causes. According to financial records, they have contributed approximately $7.3 million across these three campaigns. This funding follows two paths: direct, capped donations to the campaigns and unlimited contributions to outside super PACs that support the candidates.

The governor's race has received the largest portion of this support. The DeVos family provided $6 million to Mission Michigan, a super PAC dedicated to electing John James. This amount represents roughly two-thirds of the committee's total fundraising. The family also contributed $1 million to the Great Lakes Conservatives Fund to support Mike Rogers and provided $87,000 to Tom Barrett’s campaign.

Beyond the DeVos family, other national donors are involved. Tim Dunn, a Texas oil executive, has invested roughly $10 million into the super PAC backing Rogers. As these candidates share both donors and administrative offices, questions arise regarding their primary accountability: do they answer to the voters in their districts or to the individuals who financed their political efforts?

evidence: One family, the DeVos family of west Michigan, whose members include former U.S. Education Secretary Betsy DeVos, has given about $7.3 million across the three campaigns, plus more to the Michigan Republican Party, according to federal and state campaign-finance records.
A Texas oil executive, Tim Dunn, put roughly $10 million into the super PAC backing Rogers.
In a district like Barrett's, the person who represents Lansing in Congress and the two candidates for statewide office all draw on one short list of donors.
B1-B2.headline: Same Donors Fund Michigan Republican Ticket

pages.text: The financial architecture supporting Michigan’s 2026 Republican ticket reveals a concentrated donor base that bridges federal and state contests. Mike Rogers, seeking a U.S. Senate seat, John James, campaigning for governor, and Representative Tom Barrett, defending his Lansing-area House seat, are all beneficiaries of a remarkably consistent group of financiers. As the November 3 general election approaches, the influence of these donors remains a central feature of the political landscape.
pages.caption: Illustrative image: Lansing, Michigan skyline 2024

pages.text: The DeVos family, whose wealth originated from the direct-sales corporation Amway, serves as the primary engine for this funding. Federal and state records indicate the family has funneled approximately $7.3 million into these three campaigns, utilizing both direct contributions and unlimited super PAC expenditures. The governor’s race has seen the most significant allocation, with family members providing $6 million to Mission Michigan, the super PAC established to support John James.

This sum accounts for nearly two-thirds of the committee's total reported revenue. The pattern of shared financial support extends to the Senate and House races. The DeVos family contributed $1 million to the Great Lakes Conservatives Fund, which supports Mike Rogers, and provided $87,000 directly to Tom Barrett’s campaign.

Furthermore, the federal campaigns for Rogers and James share administrative infrastructure, utilizing the same treasurer and compliance services through the Crosby Ottenhoff Group. National interests, particularly within the energy and private-equity sectors, have also converged on these races. Tim Dunn, an executive at the Texas-based CrownQuest, has directed roughly $10 million toward the super PAC backing Rogers.

Other high-profile donors, including Stephen Schwarzman of Blackstone and Ken Griffin of Citadel, have also contributed significant sums. While these donations are legal, they highlight the intersection of private wealth and public policy. As these candidates rely on a narrow list of donors, the question of whether their legislative priorities align with their constituents or their financiers remains a subject of public scrutiny.

evidence: The DeVos family built its fortune on Amway, the west Michigan direct-sales company, and has spent four decades funding Republican candidates and school-choice causes.

The family funds every Republican at the top of the 2026 Michigan ballot, on both of the tracks the law allows: capped checks straight to the campaigns, and unlimited checks to the outside super PACs that spend on the candidates' behalf.
The single largest piece is in the governor's race.

pages.text: The Lansing City Council met on September 14. Three weeks ago, the council voted 7 to 1 to ask the city to stop using Flock Safety cameras. However, the cameras are still in the city. One person said there are at least 28 Flock cameras.
pages.caption: Illustrative image: Lansing, Michigan skyline 2024

pages.text: The mayor has not answered the council's request. The council cannot remove the cameras alone. They talked about other things instead. They had four public hearings about money and new rules. They did not vote on these items. They sent them to a committee.

The council did vote on some houses. They saved two houses from being torn down because people wanted to fix them. People came to the meeting to talk about the cameras. They said the city has no written rules for the system.
They are worried about how the cameras work. The council members said they might write a new law, but it is not ready yet. For now, the request to remove the cameras is just a note on the record.

evidence: — Three weeks ago the Lansing City Council voted 7 to 1 to ask the city to cancel its Flock Safety license plate cameras.
"At least 28 Flock cameras" remain installed across the city, one Ward 4 resident told the council.
The council cannot remove the cameras on its own, and the residents in the room know it.
A1-A2.headline: Lansing City Council Meeting: September 14, 2026

pages.text: During the September 14 Lansing City Council meeting, residents returned to demand action on the city's Flock Safety license plate cameras. Despite a 7 to 1 vote three weeks prior requesting the removal of the devices, the cameras remain active. A Ward 4 resident noted that at least 28 Flock cameras are still installed across the city.
pages.caption: Illustrative image: Lansing, Michigan skyline 2024

pages.text: Speakers expressed frustration that Mayor Andy Schor has not responded to the council's resolution. The council deferred most major decisions during the session. Four public hearings, including two developer tax breaks and a new housing fund, were referred to committee without a vote.

The council did approve a retroactive raise for a city union and decided the fate of four properties facing demolition. Two houses were spared because owners stepped forward to repair them, while the others were ordered to be torn down. Public comment focused on the lack of oversight for the camera network.

Residents cited reports that the city lacks written policies or audit logs for the system. While some council members previously discussed drafting a binding ordinance, no such document has surfaced. Until the mayor acts or the council passes a new law, the previous resolution remains only a request on the record.

B1-B2.headline: Lansing City Council Meeting: September 14, 2026

pages.text: The September 14 Lansing City Council meeting highlighted a persistent impasse regarding the city's use of Flock Safety license plate readers. Although the council voted 7 to 1 three weeks earlier to request the termination of the city's license, the cameras remain operational. A Ward 4 resident testified that at least 28 Flock cameras are still installed throughout the city.
pages.caption: Illustrative image: Lansing, Michigan skyline 2024

pages.text: The mayor, who maintains authority over city contracts under the charter, has remained silent on the matter, prompting criticism from residents who argue that the city lacks the necessary written policies or audit logs to govern such surveillance technology. Legislative progress was largely stalled, as the council deferred action on four significant public hearings.

These included the creation of a Safe and Secure Housing fund, sponsored by Council President Peter Spadafore, and two tax incentives: Brownfield Plan #92 for the former Telamon building at 416 North Cedar Street and an Obsolete Property Rehabilitation Act certificate for 418 Baker Street. The developer for the Telamon site, led by Pat Gillespie, seeks to recover costs through future property taxes. These items were referred to committee without a vote.

The council did address property maintenance, sparing two houses from demolition after rehabilitation plans were presented. However, the broader issue of surveillance remains unresolved. While some members previously indicated an intent to draft a binding ordinance, no such legislation has been introduced. Consequently, the council's earlier resolution remains a non-binding request, leaving residents to await further action from both the mayor and the committee.

evidence: A Ward 4 resident laid out the state of play in numbers.
That account matches what this outlet's own records request found : the city certified it holds no written policy governing the system and produced no audit logs of how the network is queried.
The binding ordinance two council members said in August they wanted to draft has not yet surfaced.
